etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English, from Old French contract, from Latin contractum, past participle of contrahere (“to bring together, to bring about, to conclude a bargain”), from con- (“with, together”) + trahere (“to draw, to pull”).

definitions.definition: An agreement between two or more parties, to perform a specific job or work order, often temporary or of fixed duration and usually governed by a written agreement.

quote.citation: 2013 August 10, Lexington, “Keeping the mighty honest”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8848:
quote.text: British journalists shun complete respectability, feeling a duty to be ready to savage the mighty, or rummage through their bins. Elsewhere in Europe, government contracts and subsidies ensure that press barons will only defy the mighty so far.

definitions.definition: (law) An agreement which the law will enforce in some way. A legally binding contract must contain at least one promise, i.e., a commitment or offer, by an offeror to and accepted by an offeree to do something in the future. A contract is thus executory rather than executed.
(law) The document containing such an agreement.
(law) A part of legal studies dealing with laws and jurisdiction related to contracts.
(informal) An order, usually given to a hired assassin, to kill someone.
(bridge) The declarer's undertaking to win the number of tricks bid with a stated suit as trump.

quote.text: But thou, contracted to thine own bright eyes, feed'st thy light's flame with self-substantial fuel

quote.citation: 1557, Robert Recorde, The Whetstone of Witte:
quote.text: But now in eche kinde of these, there are certaine nombers named Abſtracte: and other called nombers Contracte.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English, from Middle French contracter, from Latin contractum, past participle of contrahere (“to bring together, to bring about, to conclude a bargain”), from con- (“with, together”) + trahere (“to draw, to pull”). The verb developed after the noun, and originally meant only "draw together"; the sense "make a contract with" developed later.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To draw together or nearer; to shorten, narrow, or lessen.

quote.citation: 1674, [Richard Allestree], “Of Boasting”, in The Government of the Tongue. […], Oxford, Oxfordshire: At the Theater, →OCLC, page 168:
quote.text: We ſee in all things how deſuetude do's contract and narrow our faculties, ſo that we may apprehend only thoſe things wherein we are converſant.

quote.citation: 1830, William Wordsworth, “The Armenian Lady’s Love”, in Yarrow Revisited, and Other Poems, London:  […]  Longman, Rees, Orme, Brown, Green, & Longman, […]; and Edward Moxon, […], published 1835, →OCLC, stanza 18, page 102:
quote.text: Mutual was the sudden transport; / Breathless questions followed fast, / Years contracting to a moment, / Each word greedier than the last;  […]

definitions.definition: (grammar) To shorten by omitting a letter or letters or by reducing two or more vowels or syllables to one.
(transitive) To enter into a contract with. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
(transitive) To enter into, with mutual obligations; to make a bargain or covenant for.

quote.citation: 1589, Richard Hakluyt, The Principall Navigations, Voiages, and Discoveries of the English Nation, […], London:  […]  George Bishop and Ralph Newberie, deputies to Christopher Barker, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: We have contracted an inviolable amitie, peace, and league with the aforesaid Queene.
Many persons  […]  had contracted marriage within the degrees of consanguinity  […]  prohibited by law.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To make an agreement or contract; to covenant; to agree; to bargain.
(transitive) To bring on; to incur; to acquire.

quote.citation: 1717, Alexander Pope, “To Mr. Jervas, with Fresnoy’s Art of Painting, Translated by Mr. Dryden”, in The Works of Mr. Alexander Pope, volume I, London:  […]  W[illiam] Bowyer, for Bernard Lintot, […], →OCLC, page 391:
quote.text: Smit with the love of Siſter-arts we came, / And met congenial, mingling flame with flame; / Like friendly colours found our arts unite, / Each from each contract new ſtrength and light.

quote.text: This talent of discretion,  […]  is no where so serviceable as to the clergy, to whose preferment nothing is so fatal as the character of wit, politeness in reading or manners, or that kind of behaviour, which we contract by having too much conversation with persons of high station and eminency;  […]

quote.citation: 1848 November – 1850 December, William Makepeace Thackeray, chapter 1, in The History of Pendennis. […], volume (please specify |volume=I or II), London: Bradbury and Evans, […], published 1849–1850, →OCLC:

definitions.definition: To draw together so as to wrinkle; to knit.
